pinterest.title: Something Blue Ideas for Your Wedding: Stitched Initials, a Sapphire, a Ribbon or a Blue Garter
pinterest.description: Something blue has long been linked with loyalty and true love, and it has a habit of staying out of sight. Stitch your initials or the wedding date in blue inside a hem, cuff or jacket lining. Wear a sapphire. Wrap a pale blue silk ribbon around the bouquet stems, choose blue soles in your shoes, or keep the oldest choice of all: a blue garter. For a wedding overseas, choose blue that survives a long-haul flight.

pinterest.title: Something Borrowed Ideas: Who Lends It, What to Borrow and Why It Goes Back
pinterest.description: Something borrowed is the one item that has to go home again. It is lucky when a happily married bride has already worn it, and the veil is often singled out as the luckiest piece to borrow. Good choices: a mother's or grandmother's veil, a sister's earrings, a friend's hair comb, a grandfather's cufflinks or tie pin, or a family rosary carried rather than worn. Ask early, agree how it travels, and return it in person.

pinterest.title: Something Old, Something New, Something Borrowed, Something Blue: The Full Rhyme and Sixpence
pinterest.description: The rhyme was first recorded in 1883, as the saying of "some Lancashire friends". By 1946 it was in print with a fifth line: and a silver sixpence in your shoe. Our guide gives the full rhyme, what borrowed and blue have long stood for, how couples choose an heirloom and a piece made for the day, where the sixpence goes, and how to carry family pieces safely to a destination wedding.

slides: Something old, something new, something borrowed, something blue. Here is the full rhyme, and how to do each line well.
First recorded in 1883, as the saying of "some Lancashire friends". By 1946 it was in print with a fifth line: a silver sixpence in your shoe.
Something old: the strongest is a piece with a name attached. A grandmother's brooch, a father's cufflinks, a locket that has been to three family weddings.
Something new: the dress or suit can be enough. Or commission one piece, engraved with the date or the place, to become the next generation's something old.
Something borrowed: lucky when a happily married bride has already worn it. The veil is often singled out as the luckiest piece to borrow.
Something blue: long linked with loyalty and true love. Try initials stitched in blue, a sapphire, a ribbon on the bouquet or a blue garter.
The sixpence goes in the left shoe. Tape it inside or tuck it under the insole so it is comfortable all day.
Bringing family pieces to a wedding overseas? Send us a message and talk it through with a Wedded Advisor.
instagram_carousel.caption:
Something old, something new, something borrowed, something blue. Most couples can recite it. Fewer know it was first recorded in 1883, as the saying of "some Lancashire friends", or that by 1946 it was in print with a fifth line: and a silver sixpence in your shoe.

Something borrowed is lucky when a happily married bride has already worn it, and the veil is often singled out as the luckiest piece to borrow. Blue has long been linked with loyalty and true love. When the gown was white, the blue was carried in the garters.

Something old and something new are your own choice. Most couples wear a family heirloom, such as a grandmother's brooch or a father's cufflinks, and a piece made or bought for the wedding. A grandmother's sapphire ring, lent for the day, is old, borrowed and blue at once.

Marrying overseas? Carry heirlooms, borrowed pieces and the sixpence in your hand luggage, photograph them before you fly, and check your travel insurance's per-item limits.

Our guide covers every line of the rhyme, something blue ideas that travel well, and how to bring family pieces safely across the world.

newsletter.subject: Something old, something new: the rhyme, line by line
newsletter.preview: Where the rhyme was first recorded, something blue ideas, and how to carry family pieces overseas.
newsletter.blurb: Something old, something new, something borrowed, something blue was first recorded in 1883, and by 1946 a silver sixpence had joined it. Our new guide gives the full rhyme, what borrowed and blue have long stood for, and how couples choose an heirloom and a piece made for the day. Then it turns to the wedding overseas: something blue that survives a long-haul flight, who to borrow from, and how to carry irreplaceable pieces safely.
